newsitem.title: INDIA: Three separatist guerrillas killed in Kashmir.
newsitem.headline: Three separatist guerrillas killed in Kashmir.

text.p: Three leaders of a Moslem separatist group were killed in a shootout with paramilitary soldiers, police in India's Jammu and Kashmir state said on Saturday.
The early-morning gunbattle with the Hizb-ul-Mujahideen guerrillas erupted in the Manabal suburb of Kashmir's summer capital Srinagar, police said.
But separatist leaders accused Indian security forces of killing the guerrilla leaders in custody. Police denied the charge.

"On March 5, Indian security forces arrested senior militant leaders from Abi-Guzar locality of Srinagar...and later killed them in custody," Mohammad Yasin Malik, a senior official of All Parties Hurriyat Conference told journalists.
Hurriyat bands more than 30 Kashmiri separatist groups.

"There is no truth in these allegations, three activists of Hizb-ul-Mujahideen were killed in an encounter when they were holding a meeting," A. K. Suri, additional director general of Jammu and Kashmir Police, told Reuters.
"This has crippled the backbone of the Hizbul. It is a major success," Suri said.
He named the three guerrilla leaders as Firdous Kirmani, Manzoor Ahmed Malik, and Abdul Majid Wani.
It was the second time in three days that Kashmir police have struck against the Hizb-ul-Mujahideen, one of more than a dozen separatist groups operating in the Himalayan region.

On Friday, police and separatists said Mohammad Yousuf Ganie, deputy chief commander of the Hizb-ul-Mujahideen, was killed in a gunbattle near Anantnag town, 60 km (35 miles) south of Srinagar on Thursday evening.
The Mujahideen said in a written statement that Ganie was tortured to death by Indian security forces.
On Friday evening, a Hizb-ul-Mujahideen statement sent to local newspaper offices said Kirmani, Malik and Wani had been captured from a Srinagar hideout and the group feared they would be killed.
Hizb-ul-Mujahideen is fighting for merger of the Himalayan state with neighbouring Pakistan.
Police and hospital officials say more than 20,000 people have been killed in a seven-year-old separatist rebellion in mostly Hindu India's only Moslem majority state.
Two of the three wars fought between India and Pakistan since they gained independence in 1947 have been triggered by disputes over the Kashmir region.
The surge in Kashmir violence occurred as India and Pakistan prepare to resume stalled peace talks later this month.

Pakistan announced on Thursday that foreign ministry secretaries of the two governments would meet in New Delhi on March 28-31, and Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda said he hoped to see a positive outcome from the exercise.

The last round of talks between the South Asian neighbours was in January 1994. They bogged down owing to differences over Kashmir, two-thirds of which is controlled by India and the rest by Pakistan.
New Delhi regards all of the region as an integral part of the Indian union.

But Islamabad, which denies New Delhi's charges of training and arming the rebels, wants the Kashmiris to be allowed to vote in a U.N.-mandated plebiscite on whether to join Islamic Pakistan or Hindu-majority India.
No agenda has been announced for the March 28-31 meeting. Pakistan has insisted in the past that Kashmir was the "core issue" and must be on the agenda of any India-Pakistan dialogue.
